slides.title: Conceptual Queue

blocks.text: A queue is a collection whose elements are added at one end
(rear of queue) and removed from the other (front of queue).
The elements processed in a first in, first out (FIFO) manner.
Example: waiting line in a bank, or cars at a red light.

(rear of queue) and removed from the other (front of queue).
❑The elements processed in a first in, first out (FIFO) manner.
❑Example: waiting line in a bank, or cars at a red light.

slides.title: Queue Operations

blocks.text: enqueue means add a new element to the rear of a queue.
dequeue means remove the front element from the queue.
first returns the front element but without removing it.

slides.title: Queues in the Java API

blocks.text: Java is not consistent in its implementation of collections.
The Java API provides the java.util.Stack class that implements a stack collection.
Instead of a queue class, a Queue interface is implemented by several classes including the LinkedList class.
The Queue interface does not define enqueue, dequeue, and first. Instead, it defines two alternatives versions that add and remove elements from the queue.
The two alternative versions handle exceptions differently.

❑The Queue interface does not define enqueue, dequeue, 
and first. Instead, it defines two alternatives versions that 
add and remove elements from the queue.
❑The two alternative versions handle exceptions differently.

slides.title: Methods provided by Queue<T>

blocks.text: Two methods for adding elements: add and offer.
add throws an exception if an element cannot be added.
offer returns true if adding is successful, and false otherwise.
Two methods for removing an element: remove and poll.
remove throws an exception if the queue is empty.
poll returns null if the queue is empty.
Two methods for getting first element without removing it.
element throws and exception if the queue is empty.
peek returns null if the queue is empty.

slides.title: Coded Messages

blocks.text: A Caesar cipher is a simple approach to encoding messages by shifting each letter by a constant amount k.
For example, if k is 3, the message:

simplicity follows complexity is encoded as:
vlpsolflwb iroorzv frpsohalwb
The letter x is encoded as a, y becomes b, and z becomes c
To decode a message, we subtract k from each letter.
Unfortunately, the Caesar cipher is easy to break.
There are only 26 possibilities for shifting the characters.

slides.title: Using a Repeating Key

blocks.text: The encoding can be improved by using a repeating key.
We shift each character using a list of key values.
If the message is longer, then the key values are repeated.
For example, if the key values are 3 1 7 4 2 5 then the first character is shifted by 3, the second by 1, the third by 7, etc.

slides.title: An Array Implementation of a Queue

blocks.text: If we implement a queue as we did with a stack, one end of the queue (front or rear) would be fixed at index 0.
Unlike a stack, a queue operates at both ends.
Fixing one end of the queue at index 0 is inefficient.
Requires shifting all n queued elements, which is O(n).
To be efficient, we must avoid shifting elements.

slides.raw_text:
An Array Implementation of a Queue

the queue (front or rear) would be fixed at index 0.
❑Unlike a stack, a queue operates at both ends.
❑Fixing one end of the queue at index 0 is inefficient.
▪
Requires shifting all n queued elements, which is O(n).
❑To be efficient, we must avoid shifting elements.

slides.title: A Circular Array Implementation

blocks.text: A better solution is to treat the array as circular.
If the array has 100 elements, then the last element at index 99 is followed by the first element at index 0.
We use two integer indices to keep track of the front and rear of a queue at any given time.

slides.title: Wrapping Around a Circular Queue

blocks.text: When the rear of the queue reaches the end of the array, it wraps around back to index 0.
Once an element has been added to the queue, it stays in the same location until it is removed.
No elements need to be shifted as elements are added or removed.

slides.title: Double-Ended Queue (Deque)

blocks.text: A double-ended queue is an extension of the concept of a queue that allows adding, removing, and viewing elements from both ends of the queue.
The Java Collection API provides the Deque<T> interface.
A Deque can be implemented using an array or linked list.
A Deque can be used as a Queue or Stack.
It can replace the java.util.Stack class.
